newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan reports boom in car exports in May.
newsitem.headline: Japan reports boom in car exports in May.

text.p: Japan's vehicle exports accelerated strongly last month due to the weaker yen, the car industry said on Thursday, sparking fears of worsening tension over Tokyo's trade surplus.

Booming car exports have been a key factor pushing up Japan's trade surplus, whose growth has dismayed key trading partners such as the United States and drawn increasingly tough warnings of a possible trade war.

The Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association (JAMA) said vehicle exports jumped 28.8 percent in May from the same month a year earlier to 346,532 units as the relatively weaker yen generated extra overseas demand for Japanese models.
Japan announced earlier this month that its overall trade surplus more than tripled in May, partly due to strong car exports.
The latest car export figures came on the eve of a planned meeting between America's Big Three carmakers and President Bill Clinton to discuss Japan's surplus and the car trade.
Japan's car exports have been rising on a month-on-month basis for the past year, reflecting the yen's fall. The dollar now stands at around 114 yen against about 109 yen last year.
The export figures set alarm bells ringing on trade tension, but analysts said makers would likely slow the pace of exports in the coming months to head off any serious spat.
"Japanese carmakers are now exporting without moderation. It's dangerous," said Noriyuki Matsushima, a senior analyst at Nikko Research senior analyst.
Koji Endo, a senior vice president at Lehman Brothers Japan Inc, said: "If the current growth rate continues in and after June, it will rekindle trade friction."
But he said Japanese manufacturers would restrain their exports in the future to avoid igniting a trade battle.

JAMA cited foreign exchange movements as a reason for the surge, but also said a relatively low level of exports a year earlier had exaggerated the move and predicted that the rate of growth will slow down in the coming months.
The Group of Seven (G7) leading industrial nations called at their weekend summit in Denver for Japan to keep its trade surplus in check.

President Bill Clinton on Sunday sounded a stern warning that Japan risked an economic war if its trade surplus started exploding again and the European Union has also expressed concern about the trade imbalance.
"Japan should keep shipments to Europe modest. Unlike in America, Japanese makers do not have sufficient production capacity in Europe yet," Matsushima said.
A Nissan spokesman said exports to the United States were likely to be flat in fiscal 1997/98. "Even if there is a slight gain, that would be U.S.-made cars," the spokesman said.
Nissan's exports rose 29.8 percent to 52,158 units in May, while those to the United States climbed 17.7 percent to 22,089. Nissan expects a marginal rise in shipments to the EU in 1997/98.
Although Toyota Motor has said its plans to trim car exports to the United States in 1997/98 are due to an expected dip in demand, not trade friction, analysts see a possible political motive.
"Toyota is paying close attention to not stirring up the U.S.," said Matsushima.
Toyota's exports to the United States fell 0.1 percent from a year earlier to 35,951 in May, while those to EU rose 17.7 percent to 28,831.

Unlike Japan's top two carmakers, Honda Motor is planning to boost exports to the United States to 240,000 units in 1997/98 from 183,700 a year earlier because of strong U.S. demand. Honda said this will bring exports back to the 1995/96 level.

"By autumn, it should be clear whether U.S. car production will be revised down as a result of a possible slowdown in its economy. So that is the point when Japan's exports could revive as an issue between Japan and the U.S.," Matsushima said.
